content: A variety of antifungal medications, formulations, and combinations are available for the treatment of newborn infants with either suspected or confirmed invasive fungal infections. It is important to evaluate the relative benefits and drawbacks of these treatment options. The objective of this review was to determine the effects of different antifungal drugs, formulations, or combinations on mortality and morbidity in newborn infants diagnosed with or suspected of having invasive fungal infections. To achieve this, the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group was employed. This included comprehensive searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (up to Issue 2, 2012), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL (up to March 2012). Additionally, conference proceedings and prior reviews were examined. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared one antifungal agent or combination of agents with another in newborn infants with suspected or confirmed invasive fungal infections. Data were collected and analyzed using the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Each author independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. The results were synthesized using measures such as risk ratios and risk differences. Only one small trial, involving 24 newborn infants, was identified. This trial compared the use of fluconazole with amphotericin B (with the addition of 5-fluorocytosine in cases of fungal meningitis). The trial did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in mortality between the two treatment groups (risk ratio 0.73; 95% confidence interval 0.26 to 2.05). The authors concluded that the available data are insufficient to guide clinical practice. There is a need for large, well-designed randomized controlled trials to compare the efficacy and safety of different antifungal drugs, formulations, or combinations in the treatment of invasive fungal infections in newborn infants.
